sentences.text: Rauisuchus, which translates to Wilhelm Rau's crocodile, was an extinct archosaur living in Brazil during the Late Triassic.
This animal is recognized by a knob-like swelling on the front of its upper jaw, short neck bones with ridges underneath, and long tail vertebrae with distinct spines.
It belongs to the Rauisuchidae family, a group of land-dwelling relatives of crocodiles, although it was once placed in the Theriodontia in 1936.
Members of this group were apex predators that consumed other reptiles and may have hunted early dinosaurs.
Rauisuchus forms a specific evolutionary branch alongside Tikisuchus and Yarasuchus.
Dr. Wilhelm Rau found the remains near the road from Santa Maria to San Jose in 1928 or 1929 while working for Friedrich von Huene.
The site, called Zahnsanga, sat twenty to thirty meters from the road and was likely a ravine or steep cliff.
Krebs described the ankle bone of R. tiradentes in 1973, and the official type specimen was designated in 1976.
In 2014, Lautenschlager and Rauhut excluded remains from Locality 15 because they could not be clearly identified as Rauisuchus.
The creature inhabited what is now the Paleorrota Geopark in Brazil during the middle Triassic, between 240 and 230 million years ago.
However, the total time range for the genus spans from the Carnian to the Norian stages, between 237 and 205.7 million years ago.
